one_liner: Friendly Captcha's BLAKE2b proof-of-work solver in AssemblyScript WASM, claimed an order of magnitude faster than its own JS fallback.
what_it_does: Solves Friendly Captcha v1 puzzles: a 32-64 byte puzzle buffer is zero-padded to one 128-byte block and the solver increments a 32-bit counter in bytes 124-127 until the first 4 bytes of BLAKE2b-256 (little-endian u32) fall below a difficulty threshold; n such solutions are concatenated. It ships two builds with the same call shape, getWasmSolver(module) and getJSSolver(), each returning solve(puzzleBuffer, threshold, n) -> [solution, hash]; the friendly-challenge widget picks WASM and falls back to JS when WebAssembly fails to initialise. It is a component of that widget, not a general hashing library.
how_it_is_fast: The WASM path (src/blake2b/blake2b64.ts) runs BLAKE2b on native i64 adds and rotr with the 16 working words held in locals, the G function unrolled for all 8 column/diagonal mixes, SIGMA read from a static memory segment, unchecked loads and --noAssert -O3. Per attempt it only resets the 8-word chain value and compresses a single final block read straight from the caller's buffer as 16 u64 loads, with no allocation. The JS fallback (src/blake2b/blake2b.ts, adapted from dcposch's CC0 blake2b.js) must emulate every 64-bit add and rotate with pairs of 32-bit words in Uint32Arrays and re-reads the 128-byte block byte by byte each attempt, which is where the WASM build's advantage comes from.
when_to_use: You are integrating or auditing Friendly Captcha v1 (friendly-challenge) and need to know which solver a client ran (diagnostics byte 0: 1 = JS fallback, 2 = WASM).
You want a compact reference for a single-block BLAKE2b PoW inner loop in AssemblyScript, using native i64 and locals instead of 32-bit word-pair emulation.
Browser or web-worker PoW where the input is exactly one 128-byte block and only a 4-byte counter changes per attempt.
Studying how much a 64-bit-arithmetic hash gains from WASM over JS: the repo holds both implementations plus a 32/64-bit equivalence test (test/blake2b64.astest.ts).
when_not_to_use: As a general BLAKE2b library: the solver path assumes an unkeyed, single 128-byte block and skips buffer resets ('Danger: ... only possible because our input is exactly 128 bytes').
When you need an OSI licence: the README states 'Friendly Captcha License; source-available only' and there is no LICENSE file at the root.
When you need maintained tooling: last commit 2022-12-01, pinned to AssemblyScript ^0.16.1 with a hand-pruned loader, and the README warns an upgrade needs loader changes.
Browsers or hardened modes without WebAssembly or with the JIT off: the JS fallback is the path that runs there, and it is the slow one (maintainer's slowest JS figure: 170k hashes/s).
When you need published, reproducible speed numbers: the WASM vs JS ratio has never been measured on one machine in the repo.

integration.form: module (npm package friendly-pow 0.2.2; WASM embedded as base64 through wasmwrap)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime; build needs assemblyscript ^0.16.1, wasmwrap, TypeScript 3.x, as-pect and jest
integration.min_toolchain: Browser or Node with WebAssembly MVP (i64, no SIMD or threads) for the WASM path; any ES5-era engine with typed arrays and DataView for the JS fallback
integration.platforms: any JS engine; WASM path needs WebAssembly
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each WASM instance keeps one shared 128-byte input array, so one solver per worker (friendly-challenge runs one per Web Worker)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the WASM and JS solvers share one interface and are interchangeable, but the JS solver mutates the caller's buffer while the WASM solver returns views into its own linear memory

gotchas: WASM loop bound wraps: solverWasm.ts computes end = start + n in u32, so with the API default n = 4294967295 any nonzero starting counter in bytes 124-127 makes end < start and the call returns an empty 'no solution' array after zero attempts. friendly-challenge is unaffected because the wrapper copies the caller's untouched buffer (counter 0) into WASM memory each call; direct callers resuming from a nonzero counter are not.

Built with --runtime stub, so nothing is ever freed: every solve call allocates a fresh Context (including an unused 128-byte b buffer) and a result array, and __release is a no-op, so memory grows with each call in a long-lived instance. The returned solution and hash are views into WASM memory and are overwritten by the next call; copy them first.

The JS solver checks a global ASC_TARGET (friendly-challenge sets self.ASC_TARGET = 0 before use); without it, reaching a solution throws a ReferenceError. It also writes the nonce through new DataView(input.buffer) at offset 124, ignoring byteOffset, so a subarray input gets the wrong bytes overwritten.

The only speed evidence in the repo is test assertions: WASM must exceed 1,250,000 hashes/s ('I hit 2.3M/s on Ryzen 3900X', test/solver.astest.ts) and JS must exceed 50,000 hashes/s (test/solver.test.ts, no machine). These are pass thresholds, not measurements, and their 25x ratio is not a speedup. The 'Can solve over and over' test is degenerate: after the first call the input keeps the found nonce, so 999 of 1,000 calls succeed on their first attempt.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over long.js (also a WASM fast path behind its own JS fallback with a no-numbers 'twice as fast' claim) only if your workload is BLAKE2b proof-of-work. superfasthash and galois carry actual measured WASM-vs-JS tables (1.21x and about 9x on additions), so they are better evidence of what AssemblyScript buys; friendly-pow is the production-deployed example with no measured ratio.
verified_claims_summary: The README's 'order of magnitude faster in most browsers' has no numbers. First-party figures exist only in issues and tests, never on one machine: issue #1 (2020) gives about 3M hashes/s for WASM on a powerful desktop vs 170k hashes/s as the slowest JS fallback seen and says WASM could cut solve time 5-10x on an old phone; PR #2 (Node 12.13.1) took the WASM solver from about 2.25M to 4.0M hashes/s after MaxGraey's unrolling; a test comment records 2.3M/s on a Ryzen 3900X.
status_note: Abandoned since 2022-12-01 (two dependabot PRs left open) and source-available under the Friendly Captcha License, so reference only. The evidence stays directional because no same-hardware JS-vs-WASM hash rate was ever published, though issue #1 and PR #2 give first-party absolute WASM hash rates.
